You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Winepress

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the winepress functions primarily as a symbol of divine wrath and eschatological judgment: the crushing of grapes and the flow of red juice picture God (or the Messiah) trampling the wicked, whose blood flows out like wine. The image is treated as one of the Bible's most vivid pictures of God's final judgment on the nations.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 63:1-6 ('I have trodden the winepress alone... their blood spattered my garments')",
    "Revelation 14:19-20 ('the great winepress of the wrath of God... blood flowed out of the press')",
    "Revelation 19:15 ('he treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty')",
    "Joel 3:13 ('Come, tread, for the winepress is full... for their wickedness is great')",
    "Lamentations 1:15 ('the Lord has trodden as in a winepress the virgin daughter of Judah')"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Christological/passion reading: the winepress as a figure of Christ's suffering — Christ himself crushed like the grape on the cross, or the solitary treader of Isaiah 63 read as the suffering Redeemer. Prominent in patristic and medieval exegesis (Augustine, medieval 'mystic winepress' iconography) and in some hymnody, though modern critical scholarship treats Isaiah 63 as a judgment text.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 63:3 read typologically of Christ ('I have trodden the winepress alone')",
        "Association with Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36; the name meaning 'oil press,' extended by devotional writers to the pressing/crushing of Christ)",
        "Isaiah 53:5,10 combined with the pressing imagery in devotional tradition"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Abundance, blessing, and covenant prosperity: full winepresses as a sign of God's favor and agricultural blessing; empty or failed presses as a sign of curse or lament.",
      "basis": [
        "Proverbs 3:10 ('your vats will overflow with new wine')",
        "Joel 2:24 ('the vats shall overflow with wine and oil')",
        "Deuteronomy 15:14; 16:13 (winepress in contexts of provision and festal joy)",
        "Haggai 2:16 and Isaiah 16:10 (failed presses as judgment/lament, the negative counterpart)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The winepress in the vineyard parables as part of God's careful provision for Israel/the church — an element of the vineyard God prepares, with Israel's failure to produce fruit leading to judgment; the press itself is incidental furniture rather than the central symbol.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 5:1-2 (God hews out a wine vat in his vineyard)",
        "Matthew 21:33 / Mark 12:1 (parable of the tenants: the owner 'dug a winepress')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Oppression, fear, or concealment in narrative settings — e.g., Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress to hide from Midian, sometimes moralized as living under oppression or acting in fear; occasionally the treading of the press is used for toil and exploitation.",
      "basis": [
        "Judges 6:11 (Gideon threshing wheat in the winepress)",
        "Job 24:11 (the oppressed 'tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst')",
        "Nehemiah 13:15 (treading winepresses on the Sabbath)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Allegorical readings of the Psalm titles 'according to the Gittith' (possibly 'upon the winepresses'), used by some patristic writers to read Psalms 8, 81, 84 as winepress psalms about the church or the passion.",
      "basis": [
        "Superscriptions of Psalms 8, 81, 84 (LXX 'for the winepresses'), allegorized by Augustine and others"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a clearly recognizable consensus: across commentaries, dictionaries of biblical imagery, and popular teaching, the winepress is above all the image of God's wrath trodden out in judgment (Isaiah 63; Joel 3; Revelation 14 and 19). The main interpretive divergence concerns Isaiah 63:1-6: historic Christian tradition often read the lone treader as Christ in his passion (giving the winepress a redemptive-suffering sense), while most modern exegesis reads it as the divine warrior executing judgment, with the New Testament (Revelation 19) applying that judgment role to the returning Christ. The 'abundance/blessing' sense is well attested in the literal agricultural texts but is secondary as a symbol. No party disputes that the term carries strong symbolic freight; the debate is over which passages control the symbol, not whether one exists."
}

The object does not carry that meaning in every passage, however; in wisdom, agricultural, and restoration texts it often signifies prosperity or is simply part of ordinary vineyard imagery."

BOOK ENTRY
The vineyard's reckoning — where the fruit a people has borne is pressed out and rendered to the Owner, in one of two vintages: presses that “burst out with new wine” when the grapes are good; the growers themselves trodden — “the great winepress of the wrath of God” — and blood for wine, when the vintage is wickedness.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 5:2 — And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
Isaiah 5:7 — For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.
Proverbs 3:10 — So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
Joel 2:24 — And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil.
Joel 3:13 — Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
Lamentations 1:15 — The Lord hath trodden under foot all my mighty men in the midst of me: he hath called an assembly against me to crush my young men: the Lord hath trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah, as in a winepress.
Isaiah 63:3 — I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
Revelation 14:19 — And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God.
Revelation 14:20 — And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
